newsitem.title: USA: Missouri joins tobacco industry lawsuits.
newsitem.headline: Missouri joins tobacco industry lawsuits.

text.p: The State of Missouri added its name Monday to the growing list of municipalities suing the tobacco industry to recover public money spent treating smoking-related illnesses.

In a lawsuit filed in St. Louis City Circuit Court, Missouri Attorney General Jay Nixon also accused the industry of violating state laws by illegally targeting children through advertising, and of lying to consumers about the health effects of tobacco use and the addictiveness of nicotine.

"By purposely misleading the public about the health risks of tobacco and implementing campaigns to addict young smokers during their valuable teen years, the companies have engaged in ongoing violations of Missouri laws," Nixon said in a statement.
"The companies have shamelessly targeted our young people to create a 'replacement' market for the smokers who are dying at a rate of 1,200 a day," Nixon said.
Nixon said he will seek civil penalties, damages and reimbursements for the millions of dollars his state spends annually for health costs attributable to tobacco.

Defendants named in the lawsuit include: Philip Morris Cos Inc ; R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Co, a unit of RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp ; American Tobacco Inc; Brown & Williamson Tobacco Corp, a unit of B.A.T Industries Plc ; B.A.T Industries Plc; British American Tobacco Co Ltd; Liggett & Myers Inc, a unit of Brooke Group ; Lorillard Tobacco Co, a unit of Loews Corp ; United States Tobacco Co, a unit of UST Inc.

The suit also names the public relations firm of Hill & Knowlton Inc and industry lobby groups such as the Council for Tobacco Research USA Inc, Smokeless Tobacco Council Inc and the Tobacco Institute.

Mississippi became the first state to try to recoup Medicaid costs of smokers when it filed suit against the industry in May 1994. At least 26 other states and municipalities like New York City and Cook County, Illinois, have have filed similar lawsuits since then.
